1	# Task 11: Pendulum wall clock with escapement
2	
3	Build a single-page browser app with the provided framework, served by vite, rendering to the canvas with id #app. Show a freestanding grandfather-style pendulum clock built only from simple geometric shapes: a tall wooden case, a round clock face with 12 hour marks, hour, minute and second hands, and a swinging pendulum with a weighted bob behind a glass-like opening. The pendulum must swing back and forth with a period of 2 seconds (one full left-right cycle), with eased motion that is slowest at the extremes. The second hand must advance in one tick per second, and the minute and hour hands must show the real current local time. Also add two small hanging weights that sink very slowly. 1	# three.js asset bridge (`aura3d import-three`)
2	
3	Carry procedural three.js content into an Aura3D project as a typed asset plus editable Aura3D source, instead of
4	porting it by hand. The bridge carries assets, animation clips, simple shaders, lights, camera and renderer output.
5	Behaviour (input, physics, scoring, UI) stays native Aura3D code. It is a build-time tool: `three` is a dev
6	dependency of your project, never a runtime dependency, and the shipped route imports only `@aura3d/engine`.

content.thinking:
I'm wondering whether the clock's moving parts (hands, pendulum, weights) need to be separate native nodes I can address at runtime, or if I can just build the whole scene in three.js and import it while still being able to mutate specific nodes by id afterward. I think the plan is to name the groups explicitly in the recipe, import it, then check what nodeIds are exposed so I can drive the animation at runtime.

I'm sketching out the clock's geometry: a plinth base, a trunk section housing the pendulum behind a glass pane, and a hood at the top with a round face, hour marks, and hand pivots. For motion, the pendulum could use a looping clip animation, but the second hand and slowly sinking weights need runtime-driven updates since their timing isn't a simple fixed loop.

Now I'm working through the physical layout math—pivot height, rod length, bob radius, and swing amplitude—to make sure the pendulum's arc doesn't collide with the weights hanging on either side, adjusting the case width and interior spacing to give enough clearance.

I'm also setting up the scene geometry: a case with set depth, a wall placed behind the clock, a floor plane, and figuring out which camera setup to use.

For motion, I'll use a sinusoidal easing function for the pendulum swing with a two-second period, driven by real time. For the hands, I'll compute the second hand's angle from the clock's seconds value rotating clockwise about the z-axis, and work out how to smoothly derive the minute hand's position from minutes and seconds.

Now I'm planning the clock face layout: positioning the hands at slightly offset z-depths within pivot groups, and designing the hood and face details—dimensions for the hood box, an inset cream disc with bezel, and hour marks placed radially around the dial with larger marks at the cardinal positions.

For the glass and case body, I'm sketching a semi-transparent material for the front pane and the trunk's panel structure—back panel, side rails, and front frame pieces sized to form the clock's case around the glass insert.

Now I'm working out the plinth, rail, and opening dimensions so the glass window sits correctly within the case, then placing the pendulum rod and bob beneath the pivot point at the right length and position.

The hood section goes above the trunk as a box with a crown piece and small finial sphere on top, and I'm planning the weights as grouped chains with cylindrical weight bodies so moving each group shifts both parts together.

For the chains, I want them long enough to disappear up into the hood interior so the top never shows past the top rail, with the weight group origin centered on the weight body and the chain extending upward from there.

For the lowering animation, I'll compute a slow time-based offset using modulo so the weight descent wraps smoothly and rewinds periodically instead of drifting indefinitely.

Now I'm picking the material palette — warm wood browns, cream for the clock face, brass for metal accents — and setting up lighting with a warm point light inside the trunk plus ambient and directional fill for the scene. I'm also placing a wood-textured floor plane and a wallpapered back wall, then positioning the camera to frame the clock nicely with a moderate field of view.

Checking the camera's field of view against distance to make sure the full clock height fits in frame, then adjusting position and target slightly higher to center it better. I'll also make sure each mesh in the scene has a unique name.

The app is a freestanding pendulum clock, and it builds and renders in headless Chrome. Typecheck passes, the render reports no errors, and the screenshot shows the whole clock. I did not check the motion or the hand positions against the real time beyond that one frame.

- **Case and room:** The wooden case, plinth, hood, cream dial with 12 hour marks, glass-fronted pendulum opening, wall, floor and warm lights come from `recipes/clock.mjs`. It was imported with `import_three`, which generated `src/three-bridge/clock.bridge.ts`. The camera is front-facing and slightly above center.
- **Moving parts:** The hands, pendulum and weights are native Aura3D nodes added in `src/three-bridge/clock.scene.ts`, with runtime ids so `src/main.ts` can drive them each frame. I did this because the bridge's node transforms are load-time only. The recipe can still bake in rest-pose copies with `includeMoving: true`.
- **Pendulum:** It swings sinusoidally with a 2-second period and an 11° amplitude, so it is slowest at the extremes.
- **Hands:** The second hand jumps once per second from the local clock. The minute and hour hands show the real local time.
- **Weights:** Two weights sink at 0.004 and 0.0027 m/s. Each snaps back up after 0.35 m, because a continuous descent would leave the case within a minute or two.
- **Readiness:** `window.__EVAL_READY__` is set on the first frame callback, not after `app.ready()` resolves. The render diagnostics reported the frame as drawn.
- **Debug state:** `window.__TASK_STATE__` exposes the current swing angle, time and weight heights.

input.summary:
I added a "Lights off" button below the canvas. Clicking it switches to a dim night look and relabels it "Lights on"; clicking again restores the warm lighting. Typecheck passes. I rendered the night look once, with the default temporarily flipped to lights off: the dial, hands and pendulum stayed readable in a dim warm pool. I then raised the night ambient light from 0.5 to 0.9 so the room isn't pure black, and I did not re-render after that change. I did not click the button in a browser; the lights-on frame was only checked before the night-lighting rewiring, and the button's click handler wasn't exercised.

- **How it switches:** the four warm lights from the bridge (`clockLights()`) now have runtime ids and are hidden when lights go off. A night set is shown instead: a cool dim ambient light, a faint warm light on the dial, and a faint glow inside the case. The changes are in `src/three-bridge/clock.scene.ts` and `src/main.ts`.
- **State:** `window.__TASK_STATE__` is now exactly `{ lightsOn, pendulumAngleDeg }`, updated every frame. `pendulumAngleDeg` is the signed angle from vertical in degrees, with a peak of ±11°. I removed the earlier time and weight fields from that object.
